title: Recovery of Inflammation, Cardiac, and Muscle Damage Biomarkers After Running a Marathon
authors: Bernat-Adell MD, Collado-Boira EJ, Moles-Julio P, Panizo-Gonzalez N, Martinez-Navarro I, Hernando-Fuster B, Hernando-Domingo C
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 86 marathon runners, repeated blood sampling 24 h before the race, immediately after and at 24, 48, 96 and 144 postrace hours (results quote 192 h)
findings: Lactate dehydrogenase increased and differed from baseline at all times (p <= 0.001), normalising after 192 hours (p = 0.667).
Creatine kinase was elevated significantly up to 96 hours and normalised after 144 hours.
High-sensitivity troponin T was elevated at the finish, 24 and 48 hours, normalised after 96 hours, but showed a new significant value at 192 hours (p <= 0.001).
C-reactive protein was significantly elevated at the finish and at 24, 48, 96, 144 and 192 hours.
Recovery varies by biomarker; greater energy expenditure increased LDH, CK and hs-TNT, and blood levels decreased with longer race times.
limitations: The abstract's methods list sampling to 144 h, while its results report 192 h values (internal inconsistency); biomarkers are not performance or function; no running or training data after the race; recreational marathoners only.
implications: After a marathon, circulating markers do not all normalise inside 7 days (LDH at about 8 days, CRP still elevated at 8 days), so a 7-day full-stop is not justified by biochemistry alone; it is a convention.
Supports a graded return rather than a binary release: CK clears by about day 6 while CRP stays elevated longer, which argues for capped intensity in week 2 after a marathon.
The late hs-TNT value at 192 h is unexplained in the abstract; do not build a rule on it.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed author lists match. Abstract re-read (PMID 31045685); LDH 192 h p = 0.667, CK 96/144 h, hs-TNT, CRP and the energy/race-time statements match. Sampling-time inconsistency in the abstract confirmed.
